To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HBV infection can promote angiogenesis by regulating the expression of angiogenesis‐associated protein, which is a novel mechanism of hepatocellular carcinoma development.
HBV replication induces angiogenesis in hepatocytes and that HBV‐inducible angiogenesis can be evaluated by quantitative proteomics based iTRAQ.

iTRAQ‐based 2‐D proteomics analysis of HBV replicating rat primary and HepG2 hepatocytes identified several angiogenesis‐related proteins, including fumarate hydrase and tryptophy‐tRNA synthase, that may contribute to HBV‐induce hepatocellular carcinoma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of HBsAg expression on angiogenesis in HepG2 cells and RPHs.
the effects of HBsAg and HBeAg on angiogenesis.
the effects of HBsAg and HBx on liver angiogenesis and may lead to novel antiangiogenic hepatocarcinoma therapy based on tumor vasculature targeting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HBV replication‐related angiogenesis is associated with a number of proteins that are involved in angiogenic pathways, including the fumarate hydrate and tryptophan‐tRNA synthase.
HBV replication‐mediated angiogenesis may be associated with angiogenic enzymes, including fumarate hydrate and tryptophan‐tRNA synthase.
HBV replication‐associated angiogenic proteins identified by proteomics analysis in this study can provide novel insight into the HBV‐mediated hepatocellular carcinoma development and progression.
